title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
edition_analyzed: Original first edition, with modern references as necessary
target_audience: General readers interested in economic theory and history
core_themes: Role of self-interest and invisible hand in economic prosperity
Function of government in economic affairs
primary_purpose: To explain the fundamental principles of economic prosperity, detail the mechanisms that drive wealth creation and distribution within societies, and critique prevailing economic policies of Smith’s time, particularly mercantilism.

structure_format.narrative_style: Scholarly, methodical, and argumentative; uses case studies, historical examples, and logical reasoning
structure_format.organization: Divided into five books, each addressing different facets of economic theory: production and distribution, nature of wealth, economic history, policy, and public finance

key_concepts_lessons: The division of labor drastically increases productivity and economic efficiency.
Free competition and individuals’ pursuit of self-interest leads, as if by an ‘invisible hand’, to societal prosperity.
Wealth comes from the productive labor of individuals, not amassing gold or strict state regulation (mercantilism).
Market prices and value are determined by labor and utility, not merely by state edict.
The government has three primary functions: defense, justice, and public works not profitable for private enterprise.
Excessive regulation stifles innovation and economic growth.
style_tone: Occasionally polemical in critique of alternatives
notable_features: Laid the foundation for modern economic theory
Introduced the concept of the ‘invisible hand’
Enduring influence on global economic policy
Comprehensive integration of economics into social philosophy
cultural_historical_context: Published on the eve of the Industrial Revolution and the American Revolution, the book responded to 18th-century debates about the role of the state, commerce, and emerging capitalist economies. Smith’s insights challenged dominant mercantilist thinking and profoundly influenced subsequent economic development and policy worldwide.
reception_impact: Regarded as the foundational text of classical economics
Influenced economic policy, liberal market reforms, and academic economics
Widely cited by economists, historians, and political theorists
Debated and critiqued for limitations on labor theory of value and neglect of class/structural analyses in later scholarship
comparable_titles: The Theory of Moral Sentiments by Adam Smith
Principles of Political Economy and Taxation by David Ricardo
On Liberty by John Stuart Mill
